Scale a training run across multiple GPUs with distributed data parallel, handling seeding, samplers, and checkpointing correctly

nodes.title: Quality Engineering & Test
nodes.overview: Keeping a manufactured product inside spec using statistics. Statistical process control (SPC) watches a line's drift, capability indices quantify margin, and reliability testing (accelerated life, HALT/HASS) predicts field failures before customers find them.
proficiency: Set up an SPC control chart and act correctly on out-of-control signals
Compute process capability (Cpk) and translate it into an expected defect rate
Design an accelerated life test and defend the acceleration model
Run a root-cause investigation (8D, fishbone) that ends in a verified fix

acquisition.notes: Statistics classes teach the math; applying it to a real line is industry work.

nodes.title: Quantum Information & Computing
nodes.overview: Quantum information studies computation and communication using quantum systems. The basic unit is the qubit, a two-level quantum system that can exist in superpositions of 0 and 1, and computations are sequences of quantum gates acting on entangled qubits. The field covers what quantum computers can do faster than classical ones, and why decoherence, the loss of quantum behavior through environmental interaction, makes building them hard. It is a specialized topic sitting at the intersection of physics, computer science, and a growing hardware industry.
proficiency: Compute the action of standard gates (Hadamard, CNOT, Pauli, phase) on multi-qubit states, by hand for small circuits.
Determine whether a given two-qubit state is entangled and compute measurement statistics for each party.
Trace through Deutsch-Jozsa and Grover's algorithm on small instances and state where the quantum speedup comes from.
Explain the quantum no-cloning theorem and derive it from linearity.
Describe how a simple error-correcting code (the three-qubit bit-flip code) detects and corrects an error without measuring the encoded state.
resources: Nielsen & Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information

nodes.title: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.overview: Quantum mechanics is the physics of atoms, electrons, and light at the smallest scales, where outcomes are probabilistic and states are described by wavefunctions. Its mathematics is linear algebra: states are vectors, measurable quantities are operators, and the Schrodinger equation governs how states evolve in time. It is the foundation for semiconductors, lasers, chemistry, and quantum computing, and it is a required core subject for any physics-adjacent engineering path.
proficiency: Solve the Schrodinger equation for standard potentials (infinite well, harmonic oscillator, hydrogen atom) and interpret the resulting energy levels.
Compute measurement probabilities and expectation values from a given quantum state using the operator formalism.
Manipulate spin-1/2 systems with Pauli matrices, including computing outcomes of sequential spin measurements.
Apply time-independent perturbation theory to compute first-order corrections to energies and states.
Compute commutators and use them to determine which observables can be simultaneously known, deriving uncertainty relations.
resources: Griffiths, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics

nodes.title: Real Analysis
nodes.overview: Real analysis is calculus rebuilt on rigorous foundations. It proves, rather than assumes, when limits exist, when functions are continuous, when sequences and series converge, and when the informal moves of calculus, such as swapping a limit with an integral, are actually valid. The key new idea is uniform convergence, a stronger notion of "functions approaching a limit" that makes those swaps legal. It is a specialized skill for most engineers but essential for anyone doing theoretical work in optimization, probability, or numerical analysis.
proficiency: Prove convergence or divergence of a given sequence or series directly from the epsilon-N definition
Prove a function continuous or uniformly continuous from the definition, and exhibit counterexamples separating the two notions
State and apply the completeness axiom, Bolzano-Weierstrass, and the intermediate and extreme value theorems in proofs
Determine whether a sequence of functions converges pointwise or uniformly and prove which limit-swapping operations are justified
Prove a bounded function Riemann integrable or not using upper and lower sums
Derive the standard theorems of calculus, such as the mean value theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus, from first principles
resources: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis

nodes.title: Reinforcement Learning
nodes.overview: Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning to act: an agent takes actions in an environment, receives rewards, and improves its policy to maximize long-term reward. The formalism is the MDP (Markov decision process), which defines states, actions, transitions, and rewards. The two main solution families are value methods, which estimate how good states and actions are, and policy gradients, which adjust the policy directly; actor-critic methods combine both. RL is distinctively fragile in practice, so the skill includes exploration strategy and reward design, where most real failures originate.
proficiency: Formalize a stated problem as an MDP, defining state, action, reward, and discount, and identify where the Markov assumption is violated
Implement tabular Q-learning and value iteration from scratch and verify convergence on a small environment
Derive the policy gradient theorem's estimator (REINFORCE) and explain how a baseline reduces variance without adding bias
Implement an actor-critic algorithm (e.g. PPO, proximal policy optimization) and get it to solve a standard continuous-control benchmark
Debug a failing RL run by separating environment bugs, reward bugs, and learning bugs, using diagnostics like value estimates and entropy curves
Predict how a proposed reward function can be gamed, produce a concrete reward-hacking scenario for it, and redesign the reward to close it
resources: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction

nodes.title: Robot Learning & VLA Models
nodes.overview: Robot learning replaces hand-written robot behavior with learned policies. The main routes are imitation learning, training on demonstrations, and VLA (vision-language-action) models, large networks that take camera images and a language instruction and output robot actions, exemplified by pi0-class architectures. World models, networks that predict how the environment evolves, support planning and simulation-based training. Like language models, robot policies are now built in stages, pre-training on broad data, mid-training on robot-relevant data, and post-training on the target task. This is a frontier node that assumes RL, vision, and classical robotics.
proficiency: Implement behavior cloning on a demonstration dataset and diagnose compounding-error failures, applying a fix such as DAgger (dataset aggregation)
Fine-tune a pretrained VLA model on a new task's demonstrations and evaluate success rate on the real or simulated robot honestly, with held-out conditions
Explain how a pi0-class architecture connects a vision-language backbone to continuous action output, including the action-generation head
Train or adapt a world model on interaction data and demonstrate it supports rollout prediction or policy improvement
Design the data mix and evaluation protocol for a pre/mid/post-training pipeline for a robot policy, and justify each stage's data
Take a policy from simulation to hardware, identifying the sim-to-real gaps (dynamics, perception, latency) and measuring the transfer loss

acquisition.notes: Moves fast; papers and lab work over any class.

resources: Black et al., pi0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control (2024)
Chi et al., Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion (2023)
Brohan et al., RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control (2023)
Ha & Schmidhuber, World Models (2018)

nodes.title: RTL Design (Verilog/FPGA)
nodes.overview: Register-transfer level (RTL) design means describing hardware as data moving between registers on each clock edge, written in a hardware description language such as SystemVerilog. The text looks like code but describes parallel circuits, not sequential instructions, so the core skill is thinking in terms of what circuit the synthesis tool will build. An FPGA (field-programmable gate array) is a reconfigurable chip that lets you deploy and test RTL without fabricating silicon. This skill is the working language of digital hardware engineering, one level above raw gates.
proficiency: Write synthesizable SystemVerilog for a pipelined datapath and state machine, and predict the registers and logic the synthesis tool will infer
Identify and fix common RTL bugs such as unintended latches, blocking versus nonblocking assignment misuse, and incomplete sensitivity
Pipeline a combinational design to meet a target clock frequency and reason about the latency and throughput tradeoff
Safely move a signal between two clock domains using synchronizers or an asynchronous FIFO (first-in first-out buffer), and explain metastability
Bring a design up on a physical FPGA board, including pin constraints, timing constraints, and on-chip debug
resources: Harris & Harris, Digital Design and Computer Architecture

demos.note: Deploy a SystemVerilog design to an FPGA dev board.

nodes.title: Semiconductor Devices
nodes.overview: Semiconductor device physics explains how transistors and diodes actually work, starting from how electrons behave in silicon. The central objects are the pn junction, the boundary between differently doped regions that makes a diode, and the MOSFET (metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor), the switch that all modern chips are built from. The subject connects circuit-level component models to the physics underneath them. It is specialized: circuit designers can treat devices as black boxes, but chip design, device engineering, and fabrication all require this layer.
proficiency: Can derive the diode current-voltage characteristic from pn junction physics and explain depletion width and junction capacitance dependence on bias.
Can identify a MOSFET's operating region (cutoff, triode, saturation) from terminal voltages and apply the correct current equation in each.
Can connect datasheet parameters (threshold voltage, on-resistance, gate charge, junction capacitances) to the physical device features that set them.
Can explain how scaling device dimensions changes speed, power, and leakage, including short-channel effects that break the simple equations.
Can extract device parameters such as threshold voltage and mobility from measured current-voltage curves.
resources: Sedra & Smith, Microelectronic Circuits
Pierret, Semiconductor Device Fundamentals

classes.title: Semiconductor Devices for Energy and Electronics

nodes.title: Signals & Systems
nodes.overview: Signals and systems is the mathematical theory of how systems transform signals over time, built around linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, ones whose behavior does not change over time and scales linearly with input. Its central tools are convolution and the Fourier, Laplace, and z-transforms, which convert hard time-domain problems into simple frequency-domain algebra. It is a foundational theory course that underpins control systems, digital signal processing, communications, and much of modern measurement.
proficiency: Can compute the output of an LTI system by convolving the input with the impulse response, in both continuous and discrete time.
Can compute Fourier series and transforms of standard signals and use their properties (shifting, scaling, duality) instead of brute-force integration.
Can use the Laplace transform to solve linear differential equations and read stability off pole locations.
Can state and apply the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, predict aliasing for a given signal and sample rate, and specify the required anti-aliasing filter.
Can analyze discrete-time systems with the z-transform and design a simple FIR or IIR digital filter to a magnitude specification, verifying it in Python or MATLAB.
resources: Oppenheim & Willsky, Signals and Systems

nodes.title: Solid-State Physics
nodes.overview: Solid-state physics applies quantum and statistical mechanics to crystalline solids: how atoms arrange into lattices, how electrons moving through a lattice form energy bands, and how those bands make a material a metal, an insulator, or a semiconductor. It also covers phonons, the quantized vibrations of the lattice. It is the specialized subject that explains why transistors, diodes, and solar cells work, making it the physics backbone of the semiconductor industry.
proficiency: Classify crystal structures by lattice and basis, and compute the reciprocal lattice used to interpret X-ray diffraction.
Derive the band structure of a one-dimensional lattice using the nearly-free-electron or tight-binding model and identify band gaps.
Compute carrier concentrations in doped semiconductors as a function of temperature and doping level.
Explain the operation of a p-n junction diode from band bending and carrier diffusion, and sketch its current-voltage curve.
Compute the phonon contribution to heat capacity using the Debye model.

acquisition.notes: Classes cover theory; device intuition builds in fab or device-engineering work.

resources: Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics

nodes.title: Sourcing & Supply Chain Logistics
nodes.overview: Getting the right parts to the right factory at the right time and cost. Covers bill of materials (BOM) management, vendor selection and audits, lead times, second-sourcing against shortages, and landed-cost thinking (tariffs, freight, inventory carrying cost).
proficiency: Build and cost a BOM, flagging single-sourced and long-lead-time parts
Qualify a second source for a critical component and define the switch criteria
Negotiate price breaks against volume commitments without stranding inventory
Trace a line-down event to its supply cause and build the buffer that prevents recurrence

acquisition.notes: Operations classes gesture at it; the skill is built inside a real supply chain.

nodes.title: Special Relativity
nodes.overview: Special relativity is Einstein's theory of how space and time measurements change between observers moving at constant speed relative to each other. It replaces absolute time with a unified spacetime, described by Lorentz transformations, and reworks momentum and energy so they stay consistent near the speed of light. It is a compact, self-contained subject that every later topic in particle physics, accelerator design, and satellite timing depends on.
proficiency: Apply Lorentz transformations to convert positions and times between reference frames and compute time dilation and length contraction.
Resolve standard paradoxes (twin, pole-in-barn) quantitatively using relativity of simultaneity.
Compute with 4-vectors, using the invariant interval and invariant mass to simplify problems.
Solve relativistic collision and decay problems using conservation of energy-momentum.
Derive the velocity addition formula and apply it to compound motion.
resources: Morin, Special Relativity: For the Enthusiastic Beginner

nodes.title: State Estimation & Filtering
nodes.overview: Inferring what a system is actually doing from noisy sensors. The Kalman filter is the exact answer for linear systems with Gaussian noise; extended and unscented variants, particle filters, and factor graphs handle the rest. Every robot, rocket, and tracking detector runs one of these in its core loop.
proficiency: Derive the Kalman filter predict and update equations from Bayesian first principles
Implement an EKF for a nonlinear system and diagnose divergence from bad linearization
Tune process and measurement noise covariances from data rather than folklore
Fuse IMU, odometry, and vision measurements at different rates into one state estimate
resources: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics

classes.title: State Estimation and Filtering for Robotic Perception
Principles of Robot Autonomy I (CS 237A, EE 260A, ME 274A)

nodes.title: Statics & Strength of Materials
nodes.overview: Statics is the analysis of structures that are not accelerating: given the loads on a bracket, truss, or frame, find the forces inside every member. Strength of materials extends this to ask whether each member survives, using stress (force per unit area) and strain (fractional deformation) to predict bending, buckling, and failure. Together they are the core analytical toolkit of structural mechanical design. Any time an engineer claims a part will not break, this is the math behind the claim.
proficiency: Can draw a correct free-body diagram for a multi-body system, including reaction forces at pins, rollers, and fixed supports.
Can solve truss member forces by the method of joints or sections and identify zero-force members by inspection.
Can compute axial, bending, and shear stresses in a loaded beam, including drawing shear and moment diagrams.
Can size a beam or column against yielding and against Euler buckling, and state which governs.
Can apply a failure criterion (von Mises for ductile metals, maximum normal stress for brittle materials) and choose a defensible factor of safety.
Can predict deflection of a cantilever or simply supported beam and verify it against a hand formula or measurement.
resources: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials

nodes.title: Statistical Inference
nodes.overview: Statistical inference is the discipline of drawing conclusions about a population or process from limited data. It covers estimators (rules for guessing unknown quantities), the bias-variance tradeoff, confidence intervals (ranges that quantify estimate uncertainty), hypothesis tests (procedures for deciding whether an effect is real), maximum likelihood (the standard recipe for fitting models to data), and the basics of Bayesian inference, which treats unknowns as having probability distributions. It is the core skill for interpreting experiments and validating models in any engineering field.
proficiency: Derive the maximum likelihood estimator for a parameter of a standard distribution and check it against method-of-moments
Compute the bias, variance, and mean squared error of a given estimator and compare competing estimators
Construct and correctly interpret a confidence interval, including stating what the confidence level does and does not mean
Design and execute a hypothesis test, choosing the test statistic, computing the p-value, and stating type I and type II error rates
Perform a basic Bayesian update from a prior and a likelihood to a posterior, and contrast the conclusion with the frequentist one
Diagnose common inference failures in a reported analysis, such as multiple comparisons, underpowered tests, or confusing significance with effect size
resources: Casella & Berger, Statistical Inference

classes.title: Introduction to Probability and Statistics for Engineers (ENGR 155C)

nodes.title: Statistical Mechanics
nodes.overview: Statistical mechanics explains the behavior of large collections of particles (gases, solids, electrons in metals) from the statistics of their microscopic states. Its central tool is the partition function, a sum over states from which temperature-dependent properties like energy, pressure, and entropy follow. It is the bridge between microscopic physics and thermodynamics, and it underlies noise in electronics, chemical reaction rates, and the physics of information.
proficiency: Compute partition functions for simple systems (two-level systems, ideal gases, harmonic oscillators) and derive energy, entropy, and heat capacity from them.
Choose the correct ensemble (microcanonical, canonical, grand canonical) for a problem and justify the choice.
Derive the Boltzmann distribution and apply it to compute occupation probabilities at a given temperature.
Apply Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein statistics to compute properties of electron gases and photon gases.
Compute entropy from counting microstates and connect it to the thermodynamic definition.
resources: Schroeder, An Introduction to Thermal Physics

classes.title: Thermodynamics, Kinetic Theory, and Statistical Mechanics I

nodes.title: Synthetic Biology
nodes.overview: Synthetic biology is the engineering of living cells: designing genetic circuits (networks of genes that switch each other on and off), assembling the DNA that encodes them, inserting it into cells through cloning workflows, and measuring whether the circuit behaves as designed. It treats DNA sequences as composable parts, the way electronics treats components. It is a specialized applied field built directly on biochemistry and molecular biology.
proficiency: Design a genetic circuit (such as a toggle switch or inducible reporter) by choosing promoters, ribosome binding sites, and coding sequences with compatible parts.

proficiency.Plan and execute a cloning workflow: design primers, amplify fragments by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), assemble them with a method such as Gibson assembly, and verify by sequencing.

proficiency: Transform assembled DNA into bacterial cells and select correct clones using antibiotic markers and screening.
Characterize a circuit's behavior with fluorescence measurements, producing dose-response curves with appropriate controls.
Diagnose a failed construct by isolating whether the fault is in design, assembly, transformation, or measurement.

acquisition.notes: Lab technique matures in a research lab, not lecture.

nodes.title: Systems Programming in C
nodes.overview: Systems programming in C means working at the level where the machine stops being abstract: pointers are addresses, memory is a flat array of bytes you manage yourself with malloc and free, and the stack and heap are real regions with real rules. It also covers undefined behavior, the class of C programs the language standard makes no promises about, and the path from source code through compilation to a running process. This node is the gate to operating systems, embedded work, performance engineering, and computer architecture, because all of them assume you can read memory diagrams fluently.
proficiency: Write correct C using pointers, pointer arithmetic, structs, and dynamic allocation, with no leaks or invalid frees under a checker such as Valgrind or AddressSanitizer
Draw the memory layout of a running process (text, data, heap, stack) and locate any given variable in it
Identify undefined behavior in a code sample (out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, signed overflow, strict aliasing) and explain what the compiler is allowed to do
Implement bit-manipulation routines (masking, shifting, packing fields) and explain two's complement and floating-point representation at the bit level
Explain what happens between typing ./a.out and main() running, including loading, and use a debugger such as GDB to inspect a crashed process
resources: Bryant & O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
Kernighan & Ritchie, The C Programming Language

classes.title: Computer Systems from the Ground Up

nodes.title: Thermal Management & Cooling
nodes.overview: Thermal management is the applied discipline of keeping things at an acceptable temperature, most often electronics. Heat moves by conduction (through solids), convection (carried by moving fluid), and radiation, and the engineer's job is to budget these paths so a chip, motor, or battery stays below its limit. It sits at the junction of thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, and electronics, and it decides whether a product needs a heat sink, a fan, or a redesign. Underestimating it is a classic way hardware products fail in the field.
proficiency: Can build a thermal resistance network from junction to ambient and compute steady-state junction temperature for a power device from datasheet values.
Can size a heat sink for a given power dissipation and airflow, and decide between natural and forced convection with supporting numbers.
Can select a fan by reading its pressure-flow curve against the system's flow impedance.
Can choose a thermal interface material (pad, paste, epoxy) and account for its resistance in the budget.
Can estimate radiation heat transfer and state when it matters (vacuum, sealed enclosures, high temperatures) versus when it is negligible.
Can instrument a prototype with thermocouples or a thermal camera and reconcile measured temperatures with the predicted budget.

acquisition.notes: Taught piecemeal; real proficiency comes from thermal design on a product.

resources: Incropera & DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer

nodes.title: Engineering Thermodynamics
nodes.overview: Thermodynamics is the physics of energy, heat, and work: what the laws of energy conservation and entropy permit, and what they forbid. In engineering it answers questions like how efficient an engine, refrigerator, or power plant can possibly be, and how much work a given heat flow can produce. It is a foundational course in the mechanical curriculum and the entry point to anything involving engines, HVAC (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning), propulsion, or energy systems.
proficiency: Can apply the first law of thermodynamics to closed and open (control volume) systems, including turbines, compressors, and heat exchangers.
Can use property tables and charts for steam and refrigerants to find state properties at each point of a cycle.
Can analyze the Rankine, Brayton, Otto, and vapor-compression refrigeration cycles and compute their thermal efficiency or coefficient of performance.
Can compute the Carnot limit for a process between two temperatures and explain why no real device beats it.
Can use entropy balances to identify where a real system loses available work relative to the ideal.
resources: Cengel & Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach

nodes.title: Transformer Architectures
nodes.overview: The transformer is the neural network architecture behind modern language models and much of vision. Its core operation is scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), which lets every position in a sequence gather information from every other position, weighted by learned relevance. Around that sit multi-head attention (several attention operations in parallel), positional encodings (since attention alone is order-blind), and two family layouts, encoder-decoder (for input-to-output mapping like translation) and decoder-only (for next-token generation like GPT-style models). The KV cache (storing past keys and values so generation does not recompute them) is the central inference-time mechanism.
proficiency: Implement scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention from scratch, including masking, and match a reference implementation numerically
Implement a KV cache for autoregressive generation and show the resulting speedup and its memory cost as a function of sequence length
Explain and implement at least two positional encoding schemes (e.g. sinusoidal, rotary) and state what breaks without one
Choose between encoder-decoder and decoder-only layouts for a stated task and justify the choice with the attention masking each implies
Compute the parameter count, FLOPs, and attention memory of a transformer configuration by hand, and explain why naive attention is quadratic in sequence length
Explain how flash attention reorders the computation to avoid materializing the full attention matrix, and when it changes what is feasible
resources: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need

nodes.title: Waves & Optics
nodes.overview: Waves and optics studies how disturbances travel through space: vibrations on strings, sound, and light. It covers coupled oscillators, the wave equation, interference and diffraction (how waves combine and bend around obstacles), lens-based optics, and Fourier decomposition, which breaks any signal into simple sine waves. It is a core mid-level physics subject and the shared language behind signal processing, imaging, acoustics, and photonics.
proficiency: Derive the wave equation for a stretched string and solve it for standing and traveling waves with given boundary conditions.
Compute normal modes and frequencies of coupled oscillator systems.
Predict interference and diffraction patterns for double slits, gratings, and single apertures, including fringe positions and intensities.
Trace rays through lens and mirror systems to locate images and compute magnification.
Decompose a periodic signal into its Fourier series and interpret the spectrum.

machines.name: Horizontal bandsaw
machines.purpose: Rough-cuts bar and plate stock to approximate length before precision work. A continuous toothed blade loop, run slow for metal with fine-pitch teeth; the horizontal form bows down through clamped stock under gravity feed.

machines.name: Drill press
machines.purpose: Drills round, perpendicular holes with a bit held in a rigid vertical spindle, lowered by lever into work clamped on the table. Also spots, countersinks, reams, and squarely starts taps. Location accuracy comes from layout and a center punch, so holes whose position is critical move to the mill instead.

machines.name: Manual mill
machines.purpose: Spins a cutter over a workpiece clamped to a table that moves on measured handwheels. Makes flat faces, squared edges, slots, pockets, and holes at precise coordinates; the machine of choice whenever a feature's location is the spec.

machines.name: Engine lathe
machines.purpose: Spins the workpiece against a fixed cutting tool, so everything it makes is rotationally symmetric and concentric with the spin axis: shafts, pins, bushings, spacers, threads. Faces ends flat, turns diameters to size, and drills perfectly centered holes from the tailstock.
